title: US Weighs Its Largest Non-Nuclear Bomb for Iran as Trump Rules Out Ground Troops, and Kyiv Breaks Openly With Washington Over Starshield and Russian Refineries
subhead: The Pentagon has drawn up strike options that include the GBU-43 'mother of all bombs' even as Trump insists no US ground troops will enter Iran, while Ukraine abandons Trump's no-strike pledge on Russian oil after a White House-ordered cut to its Starshield satellite link.

sections.heading: Washington Prepares a Bigger Bomb While Denying a Ground War
sections.body:
The US military has developed new strike options against Iran that could include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the American arsenal, according to CNN, which reported the planning on Oct 15. Reuters and The Times of Israel carried the same account, describing the plans as a significant escalation should fighting resume. The weapon, known as the 'mother of all bombs', was last used in combat in Afghanistan in 2017.

The disclosure landed the same day President Trump, in an interview with Newsmax, said he does not see the US deploying ground troops to Iran and ruled out a nuclear strike there, while questioning whether the stalled talks with Tehran can be revived. Fox News reported Tehran's response that American bombing alone will not force a surrender. The combination signals a White House trying to cap the war's cost in American lives while leaving open a much harder conventional punch.

CNN noted the planning comes as Trump faces pressure to wind down an unpopular war ahead of the November midterms. A weapon of that size is designed for deep, hardened targets, so its contemplation points to a target set - buried facilities - that smaller munitions cannot reach.
sections.whyItMatters: A publicized option to use the largest conventional bomb signals that Washington is preparing for hardened, deeply buried targets in Iran, not a winding-down. But pairing it with an explicit no-ground-troops pledge shows Trump wants escalation options that do not put Americans in combat - a narrow, fragile line.

sections.heading: Ukraine Breaks the No-Strike Deal as a White House Order Cuts Its Satellite Link
sections.body:
President Zelensky said on Oct 15 that Kyiv would no longer abide by Trump's demand not to strike Russian oil refineries, and Ukrainian drones hit a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight, according to Reuters. The Kremlin accused Ukraine of flouting the spirit of US peace efforts. Trump had declared an 'energy ceasefire' on Sunday - a deal Ukraine says it first learned about from media reports and that Russia never publicly committed to.

Behind the rupture is the sudden restriction of Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade Starlink service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and battlefield communications. Reuters, citing two US officials and a Western official, reported that the order to slow the service came from inside the White House, with the Defense Department receiving the message. AP reported that Ukrainian drone operations slowed and commanders reported lost connections. Trump's UK defense counterpart talks with US Defense Secretary Hegseth on Oct 15 welcomed the restoration of Starlink service, Reuters reported - a sign the cut is being walked back.

France's Macron said after meeting Zelensky in Brussels that it was crucial to give Ukraine all the means it needs to defend its population and infrastructure. The episode has widened a gap between Washington and its European allies just as the EU summit turned to aid for Kyiv.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the sharpest US-Ukraine rupture of the war: an ally's critical military link apparently throttled by the White House, and Kyiv retaliating by striking the Russian oil infrastructure Washington wanted spared. Whoever ordered the Starshield slowdown handed Moscow a battlefield advantage and pushed Europe to hedge against US reliability.

sections.heading: Houthi Missiles Hit Yemen's Presidential Palace in Aden
sections.body:
Houthi forces fired five missiles at the Al-Ma'ashiq presidential palace compound in Aden on Oct 15, killing at least five people, including security guards and civilian employees, and wounding 16, according to Yemen's government and Reuters. Prime Minister and cabinet members present were unharmed, Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said. The Houthi-run Saba agency said the target was a military operations headquarters run by Saudi officers at the complex, a claim Reuters could not independently verify.

The strike on the temporary seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government is a direct hit on the anti-Houthi coalition's political center. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said Houthi attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport have killed 17 people and wounded more than 330 since Oct 1, with the airport hit 20 times in two weeks. Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said the Houthis have fired 1,104 ballistic missiles and 1,135 drones at Saudi Arabia since 2016.

A Reuters analysis adds intent: the Houthi campaign against Saudi infrastructure is aimed at pressuring Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman both to meet Houthi demands in Yemen and to push Trump to ease the blockade choking Iran's economy.
sections.whyItMatters: Striking the government's own seat in Aden, not just Saudi territory, shows the Houthis can reach the coalition's political core and are deliberately tying the Yemen war to the Iran blockade. It raises the odds Riyadh escalates directly into Yemen.

sections.heading: EU Summit Splits on Energy Prices and China Trade as Kyiv Aid Advances
sections.body:
EU leaders opened a two-day summit in Brussels on Oct 15 on competitiveness, high energy prices and the bloc's next long-term budget. Reuters reported immediate wrangling over how to tame soaring energy costs, design a competitive budget, and curb surging Chinese imports blamed for job losses. Xinhua noted the first day ended with differences and the cancellation of a scheduled press conference. Politico reported leaders were turning to migration and aid for Kyiv after 14 hours of talks dominated by energy and budget splits.

The summit came on the back of an EU-China agreement to cap imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles. The Guardian reported the deal limits Chinese plug-in hybrid imports to roughly 350,000 a year, with any excess held at customs, describing it as a first step against a goods trade deficit that hit about €360 billion in 2025.

Zelensky met Macron in Brussels on the summit's margins, and France's president said Europe must give Ukraine the means to defend its infrastructure.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's two biggest economic headaches - energy costs and Chinese overcapacity - are now colliding with its security commitments to Ukraine in one budget fight. The hybrid-car cap shows Brussels is willing to use trade tools, but the summit's splits suggest funding both rearmament and industrial protection will be hard.

sections.heading: Security Council Votes Again on the Next UN Chief
sections.body:
The Security Council was expected to hold a sixth straw poll on Friday (Oct 16) for candidates to succeed Antonio Guterres, whose second term ends Dec 31, according to the Security Council Report's What's In Blue. Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan has led recent votes, Reuters reported, though El Pais noted the number of countries rejecting her has grown. Grynspan told Reuters the UN has 'become too risk-averse' and its next leader must be willing to bear the cost of diplomatic failure.

The straw polls use colored ballots - green to encourage, red to block - to gauge veto risk before any formal recommendation. The process matters because a single permanent member's red ballot can end a candidacy.
sections.whyItMatters: The choice of the next secretary-general sets the UN's posture on the Iran war, Ukraine and Gaza at a moment when the institution is being sidelined by major powers. Rising red ballots against the frontrunner show the race is still open and veto politics are hardening.

sections.heading: Pakistan School Roof Collapse Kills 33; Brazil Runoff Tightens
sections.body:
In northwest Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the death toll from a school roof collapse on Thursday rose to 33, with 17 injured discharged after observation, Xinhua reported, citing hospital and rescue officials. Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar received 53 patients, of whom 33 died and three remained under observation.

In Brazil, a Datafolha poll published Oct 15 showed Flavio Bolsonaro at 47% and President Lula at 45% ahead of the Oct 25 runoff, within the poll's two-point margin of error. The gap narrowed from 49% to 45% a week earlier, Reuters reported. A separate Quaest poll put Bolsonaro at 46% and Lula at 44%, while an Indexa/Broadcast survey had Bolsonaro at 51% of valid votes to Lula's 49%.
sections.whyItMatters: The school collapse underscores chronic infrastructure and safety failures in Pakistan's most volatile province. Brazil's tightening runoff matters far beyond Latin America: the result will shape the region's largest economy's alignment on trade, energy and relations with both Washington and Beijing.

bottomLine: The day's defining move was double-edged on Iran: the US openly weighed using its largest non-nuclear bomb while Trump ruled out ground troops and a nuclear strike, sketching a strategy of maximum conventional firepower with minimum American exposure. At the same time, the US-Ukraine alliance cracked in the open after a White House-ordered throttling of Ukraine's Starshield link and Kyiv's decision to resume striking Russian refineries against Trump's wishes, with Europe closing ranks behind Zelensky at a divided Brussels summit. Combined with Houthi missiles hitting Yemen's own presidential palace in Aden, the picture is of multiple US-led fronts where partners are hedging against Washington's reliability rather than aligning with it.
